text: Alderney Health Systems' burst-compute job is packaged the portable way Lesson nine described -- a plain Deployment and Service. Leadership wants proof it can run on both Azure and AWS, so that if the ExpressRoute-only Azure path ever becomes unavailable, the workload can fail over to AWS without a rewrite. This lab makes that proof concrete instead of theoretical.

The lab reuses the multi-cloud Terraform module from Chapter three, Lesson eleven, rather than rewriting anything. The same module source gets called twice -- once provisioning an AKS cluster, once provisioning an EKS cluster -- with identical node count and Kubernetes version passed in. The only differences between the two calls are the ones each cloud's provider genuinely requires, nothing invented out of habit.

The Deployment and Service manifest itself doesn't change at all between the two clusters, because nothing in it names a cloud. The exact same YAML file gets applied with kubectl, once against the AKS context, once against the EKS context. Same file, same command, two different clusters -- that's the real proof of portability, not a claim made on a slide.

The one place that genuinely can't stay identical is storage. Lesson nine already warned that StorageClass names aren't standardized across clouds, so rather than hard-coding one into the shared manifest, two small per-cloud values files supply it separately -- managed-csi for AKS, gp3 for EKS. The portable core stays in one untouched file; only the genuinely cloud-specific value lives in two small files that are expected to differ.

Verification closes the lab. Running the same read-only kubectl commands against both clusters -- checking the Deployment's replica count and ready status, then hitting the health check endpoint directly -- should return identical results on both sides. If they don't match, the gap is almost always in one of the known seams, a StorageClass that failed to bind or an ingress annotation the other cloud's controller ignores, not in the portable core itself.

Two labs down, and both showed hybrid and multi-cloud architecture built deliberately, for a specific reason. Lesson thirty-one flips the lens entirely, with a case study about a fictional retailer that adopted multi-cloud as a blanket policy, with no requirement and no cost model behind it, and ended up paying far more than it ever saved.
